1191.title: Clinging
1191.hook: holding on to God through the whole day
1191.howItsDone: In Hasidic teaching, devekut is pursued in prayer and also in daily activities such as eating, work and conversation, while the Talmud's teaching to walk in God's ways is lived through acts like visiting the sick and comforting mourners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no place without God: from Jacob's stone pillow to the bus stop. Your line: no place without him. Today, how to hold on in all those places.

A small child crossing a busy street holds a parent's hand. The child isn't thinking about the hand the whole time. They're chatting, pointing at a dog, counting buses. But the hand never lets go. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day." Cleave. Hold fast. The Torah asks for it more than once. The rabbis, and later the Hasidic teachers, asked the obvious question: how does a person do that, all day long, in the middle of everything else?
screen: `A HAND ACROSS THE STREET.` → `YE THAT DID CLEAVE.` → `HOW, ALL DAY LONG?`

segments.voice: Devekut. Clinging, attachment, holding on to God. First, the problem. The Torah tells the people to cleave to God. But the Talmud raises an objection. The Torah also describes God as a fire that consumes. How can anyone hold on to a fire? Second, the rabbis' answers. In one passage, the Talmud says: walk after God's ways. As God clothed the naked, clothe the naked. As God visited the sick, visit the sick. As God comforted mourners and buried the dead, do the same. In another passage, the answer is to attach yourself to the wise, to stand close to people who live by the Torah and help them. Either way, clinging to God turns into something your hands do. Third, the Hasidic turn. Hasidic teachers made devekut a center of the spiritual life, and they refused to keep it inside the synagogue. Hold on to God while praying, yes, and also while eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. Yesterday's line, no place without God, is what makes that possible. If God is in every place, then every place is somewhere to hold on. Fourth, the hand. Devekut doesn't ask a person to stop living and stare at heaven. Like the child on the street, attention can wander to a dog or a bus while the hold stays firm. A hand can slip. The practice is to notice, and take hold again. So clinging, in this tradition, is less like a grip of fear and more like walking with someone you trust, all the way across.
screen: `HOW DO YOU HOLD A FIRE?` · `WALK IN GOD'S WAYS.` · `IN EVERY PLACE, HOLD ON.` · `WHEN THE HAND SLIPS, TAKE HOLD.` · then, large: `CLING.`

segments.voice: Choose a chore, washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter, and do it slowly now, or picture doing it. As your hands work, keep one thread of attention on God, or, if that word doesn't fit you, on what you're grateful for, the way a hand is held crossing the street. When your mind wanders, come back to the thread.
Devekut. Clinging: holding on to God through the whole day, in prayer, in kindness and in ordinary work. Today's word.
Your line: cling. A hand can slip, and the practice is simply to take hold again. Until tomorrow.

1192.title: Joy opens the heart
1192.hook: Hasidism treats joy as a spiritual force, sadness as a closing
1192.howItsDone: In Hasidic communities joy is cultivated on purpose: singing wordless melodies called niggunim, dancing at weddings and festivals, and teaching that a mitzvah done gladly is done fully.

segments.voice: Yesterday, devekut: holding on to God through the whole day, even in a chore. Your line: cling. Today, what keeps the hand open.

A hand that is clenched can't receive anything. Try it right now if you like: make a fist, and then try to take a cup from someone. You can't. You have to open first. Yesterday's word asked how a person holds on to God all day long. Underneath it sits another question: what keeps a person from holding on? Hasidic teaching points somewhere you might not look first. Sadness. Heaviness. The gray mood that closes the hand. And the thing that opens it again is today's word.
screen: `A CLENCHED HAND CAN'T RECEIVE.` → `WHAT CLOSES IT?` → `HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: Simcha. Joy, gladness, the word wedding guests use when they wish a family more simchas. First, the verse. The psalm says, "Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing." Notice that gladness isn't the reward at the end of the service. It is the way the service is done. Second, the Talmud. In tractate Shabbat the sages teach that the Divine Presence does not rest on a person in the middle of sadness or laziness, but in the middle of the joy of a mitzvah. Read that way, a mood can be a door, or a wall. Third, the Hasidic turn. The early Hasidic teachers took that teaching and made it central. Joy, for them, isn't a feeling you wait for. It's a force, something that opens the heart so prayer can go up and blessing can come down. Sadness, in their language, is a closing, a contraction, and they treated it as something to work against, not something to admire. Fourth, and this matters: they didn't mean pretending. Hasidic teachers made a careful distinction. A broken heart, honest sorrow over a wrong you did, they valued. That kind of sorrow moves you. What they warned against was the heavy, stuck sadness that only sits there and closes everything. One is a door being knocked on. The other is a door locked from inside. So simcha isn't the absence of pain. It's the hand staying open, even in a hard week.

Stay with it without explaining it away or adding a but, and notice whether anything in your chest loosens. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words, serve the LORD with gladness, and let them sit.
Simcha. Joy, gladness. For the Hasidic teachers, a spiritual force that opens the heart, where heavy sadness closes it. Today's word.

1193.title: The rebbe
1193.hook: a Hasidic leader seen as guide and channel for his followers
1193.howItsDone: Hasidim visit their rebbe for blessing and advice, gather at his tish on Sabbaths and festivals to hear his teaching and sing, and often write to him with requests for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simcha: joy as the force that opens the heart. Your line: joy opens. Today, a long table on a Friday night.

A long table on a Friday night. At the head sits one man, and around him, packed shoulder to shoulder, some standing on benches, are his followers. He hardly speaks. He tastes a little of the food in front of him, and what's left is passed out into the crowd, and people reach for a crumb of it. Then someone starts a melody with no words, and the whole room picks it up. Hasidim call a gathering like this a tish, a table. The man at the head of it has a title of his own.
screen: `A LONG TABLE ON A FRIDAY NIGHT.` → `A CRUMB PASSED INTO THE CROWD.` → `THE MAN AT THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: Rebbe. It's the Yiddish way of saying rabbi, and among Hasidim it means something particular: the leader of a Hasidic community, the one his followers turn to. First, the guide. Long before Hasidism, the Mishnah gives a piece of advice in Pirkei Avot: make for yourself a teacher. Not find one, make one, as if choosing a guide is something you do on purpose. Hasidim took that seriously. A follower brings the rebbe questions about prayer, but also about a marriage, a business, a sick child. Second, the channel. Hasidic teaching speaks of the tzaddik, the righteous one, and sees the rebbe this way: someone so attached to God that blessing flows through him to the people around him, and their prayers rise with his. That's why a crumb from his plate matters to them. Third, the bond goes both ways. A rebbe carries his followers in his heart and in his prayers, and the followers' devotion is part of how the community holds together. Fourth, and fairly: not every Jew sees it this way. Some Jewish communities, from early on, were wary of giving one person that much weight, and preferred to center life on study and the rabbi as a scholar and judge. Hasidim and their critics have argued it out, and both sides would say they are guarding something precious. Here, the rebbe is met as Hasidim meet him: a guide, and in Hasidic teaching, more than a guide.
screen: `MAKE FOR YOURSELF A TEACHER.` · `A CHANNEL FOR BLESSING.` · `THE BOND GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `NOT EVERY JEW SEES IT THIS WAY.` · then, large: `A GUIDE.`

1194.title: Serving through the body
1194.hook: eating, working and resting can be worship
1194.howItsDone: Observant Jews say a blessing before and after eating, and Hasidic teaching asks that ordinary acts like eating, working and sleeping be done with the intention of serving God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebbe: the Hasidic leader at the head of the table. Your line: a guide. Today, worship outside the building.

Where does worship happen? The easy answer is a building. A sanctuary, an ark, rows of seats, a quiet hour set apart from the rest of the week. And then there's everything else: the sandwich at your desk, the dishes, the shift at work, the nap on the couch. Two lists. Holy over here, ordinary over there. The Hasidic teachers looked at those two lists and refused to keep them apart. The sandwich, they said, can be worship too. Not instead of prayer, but alongside it. Today's word is the name for that refusal.
screen: `WHERE DOES WORSHIP HAPPEN?` → `HOLY HERE, ORDINARY THERE.` → `THE SANDWICH CAN BE WORSHIP TOO.`

segments.voice: Avodah b'gashmiyut. Avodah is service, worship, the same word once used for the service in the Temple. Gashmiyut is physicality, the stuff of the body and the material world. Service through the physical. First, the verse. Proverbs says, "In all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He will direct thy paths." Hasidic teachers leaned hard on the word all. Not only in the ways that look religious. In all of them. Second, the older roots. The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot teaches that all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven. And the Talmud makes a bold comparison: while the Temple stood, the altar brought atonement, and now a person's table does. The kitchen table, set with food and with guests, takes up some of the altar's work. Third, the Hasidic turn. If God is present everywhere, then a meal eaten with a blessing before it and attention during it isn't a break from serving God. It's a way of serving. Working honestly, resting on the Sabbath, sleeping so you can rise and do good: all of it can be avodah, when it's done with the right intention. Fourth, the caution. This is not permission to call every appetite holy. The point isn't that whatever the body wants is worship. It's that the body, used with intention, can become a place where worship happens. Two lists become one.
screen: `SERVICE THROUGH THE PHYSICAL.` · `IN ALL THY WAYS.` · `A PERSON'S TABLE, LIKE AN ALTAR.` · `NOT EVERY APPETITE IS HOLY.` · then, large: `SERVE THROUGH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Think ahead to the next thing you'll eat, and see yourself pausing before the first bite: a blessing said slowly if you say one, or simply noticing where the food came from, the ground, the rain, the hands that grew it and cooked it. For now, sit with that plan, and with the plain fact of your body breathing.
Avodah b'gashmiyut. Service through the physical: the Hasidic teaching that eating, working and resting, done with intention, can be worship. Today's word.
Your line: serve through the body. Two lists can become one. Same time tomorrow.

1195.title: Bittul: dust and ashes
1195.hook: setting the self aside to make room for the divine
1195.carry: bittul: less of me, more room for god
1195.howItsDone: Hasidic teaching treats bittul as a lifelong practice of humility before God, cultivated in prayer and in ordinary dealings with others, and sees it as the ground of a person's service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah b'gashmiyut: service through the body. Your line: serve through the body. Today, bold and small at once.

Abraham is arguing with God. Two cities are about to be destroyed, and Abraham, with nothing to bargain with, keeps pressing. What if there are fifty good people there? Forty-five? Forty? He's bold. He's bargaining with the Judge of all the earth. And right in the middle of that boldness, he stops and says something about himself. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, he calls himself one "who am but dust and ashes." Bold and small in the same breath. The Hasidic teachers built a whole practice on that combination, and today's word names it.
screen: `ABRAHAM ARGUES WITH GOD.` → `BOLD.` → `AND DUST AND ASHES.`

segments.voice: Bittul. Setting aside, making void, the self stepping out of the way. In Hasidic teaching, bittul is the practice of making less of yourself so there is room for God. First, the two models. Abraham says he is dust and ashes. Moses, too, is remembered this way: the Torah says, "Now the man Moses was very meek." And when the people complain, Moses and Aaron answer, in effect, what are we? The Talmud sets those sayings side by side, as if each is a step further into getting out of the way. Second, it is not self-hatred. Abraham doesn't stop arguing because he's dust. He argues harder. Moses is meek and leads a nation. Bittul isn't thinking you're worthless. It's not making yourself the center. Third, the vessel. Hasidic teachers use the picture of a container. A cup already full to the brim has no space for what's being poured. Pour out a little of the self, and there's room. That's why yesterday's teaching and this one fit together: the body can serve, and the self can step aside so the service is for God and not for show. Fourth, the everyday version. Bittul can be as small as letting someone else's idea win in a meeting when theirs is better. Not mentioning your part in a success. Listening to the end of a sentence without preparing your reply. Small acts of less me, so that something larger has room.
screen: `DUST AND ASHES. WHAT ARE WE?` · `NOT SELF-HATRED.` · `A CUP FULL OF ITSELF CAN'T RECEIVE.` · `SMALL ACTS OF STEPPING ASIDE.` · then, large: `LESS ME.`

segments.voice: Notice how much of the inside of your head is about you, what to say, how you're coming across, what you're owed, and don't fight it; just notice its size. Then, for a few breaths, set it down like a heavy bag, and let the room, the sounds and the people you love take up the space. If you pray, you can stand before God as Abraham did, bold and small at once.
Bittul. Setting the self aside to make room for the divine. Not self-hatred: an emptier cup, with room to receive. Today's word.
Your line: bittul: less of me, more room for god. An emptier cup has more room to receive what is poured. See you tomorrow.

1196.title: Mind first
1196.hook: Chochmah, Binah, Da'at: Shneur Zalman's Hasidism of the intellect
1196.howItsDone: In Chabad, study of Hasidic teaching is part of daily life, and before or during prayer people practice contemplation, thinking carefully about an idea of God until love and awe grow from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bittul: setting the self aside to make room. Your line: less me. Today, a fire meant to last.

A spark is quick. It catches, it flares, it's gone. A coal is slow. It takes a long time to get going, but once it does, it holds its heat through the night. This week has been full of Hasidic fire: joy, clinging, the rebbe's table. One Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Shneur Zalman, wanted that fire to last. Put in a picture, his concern was the spark: a feeling that flares in prayer and is gone by breakfast. His answer begins in an odd place for a movement of the heart. With the mind. The name of his path is made of three words.
screen: `A SPARK FLARES AND IS GONE.` → `A COAL HOLDS ITS HEAT.` → `START WITH THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Chabad. It's built from three Hebrew words: Chochmah, wisdom. Binah, understanding. Da'at, knowledge. Take the first letter of each, and you have the name. First, the three belong to the Torah. When God fills Bezalel, the craftsman who builds the Tabernacle, the verse says He filled him "in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge." The same three, in the same order. Second, each one is a step. In Chabad teaching, chochmah is the first flash of an idea, the moment something clicks. Binah is the slow work of unpacking it, turning it over, building it out. Da'at is when it stops being an idea you have and becomes something you know, joined to you, so that it moves you. These are also names of the sefirot; Shneur Zalman reads them inside the person. Third, the order matters. Chabad teaches that real feeling grows from understanding. Think long and carefully about God's greatness, or God's nearness, and love and awe will come on their own, steadier than any feeling you tried to force. The head leads, and the heart follows. Fourth, it's still Hasidism. This is not cold thinking. The goal is still a heart on fire, still joy, still clinging. The mind is the way in, not the destination. The spark becomes a coal.
screen: `THREE WORDS, ONE NAME.` · `BEZALEL: WISDOM, UNDERSTANDING, KNOWLEDGE.` · `A FLASH, AN UNPACKING, A KNOWING.` · `THE HEAD LEADS, THE HEART FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `WISDOM, UNDERSTANDING, KNOWLEDGE.`

Don't chase a feeling; if one comes, let it come, and if you pray, let the thought lead you there.
Chabad. Chochmah, Binah, Da'at: wisdom, understanding, knowledge. The name of Rabbi Shneur Zalman's Hasidism, where the mind leads the heart. Today's word.
Your line: wisdom, understanding, knowledge. The head leads, and the heart follows. Rest well.

1197.title: The Tanya
1197.hook: Shneur Zalman's book on the "in-between" person, neither saint nor sinner
1197.howItsDone: In Chabad communities the Tanya is studied daily in short portions, often alongside the weekly Torah reading, and its chapters on the in-between person are taught as a guide for ordinary religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chabad: wisdom, understanding, knowledge, the mind leading the heart. That was your line. Today, the book that grew from it.

In the Talmud, a great sage named Rabbah says something about himself. The sages have just divided people into three kinds: the righteous, the wicked, and the ones in between. And Rabbah says, people like me are the in-between ones. Abaye answers, half in protest: if you are only in between, master, you leave no room for anyone else to live. That short exchange became the seed of a book. Rabbi Shneur Zalman, whose Chabad path we met yesterday, wrote it for ordinary people trying to serve God in a real life. It's known by its first word, and that word is today's.
screen: `RIGHTEOUS, WICKED, IN BETWEEN.` → `RABBAH: PEOPLE LIKE ME.` → `THE SEED OF A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Tanya. It's the opening word of the book, an Aramaic word that introduces a teaching of the sages. The book is also called Likkutei Amarim, collected sayings. First, its promise. The title page leans on a verse from Deuteronomy: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very near. Not only for saints. The book sets out to show how. Second, the twist. The in-between person, the beinoni, is not who you'd expect. You might think it means someone who sins half the time and does good the other half. The Tanya says no. Its beinoni never actually does the wrong thing, in deed or word. The struggle is all inside. The pull is still there every day, the bad thought still rises, and every day it is not obeyed. Third, the comfort. If that inner pull never goes away, it doesn't mean you're failing. That is simply what the in-between life feels like. And the Tanya presents this level as one within reach, not reserved for rare souls. Fourth, the week. Look at this week's threads: clinging to God through a chore, joy that opens, a rebbe who guides, the body that serves, the self that steps aside, the mind that leads. The Tanya ties threads like these into a plan for an ordinary day, for a person who is neither saint nor sinner, and still at work.
screen: `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.` · `NOT HALF GOOD, HALF BAD.` · `THE PULL STAYS, AND IS NOT OBEYED.` · `THIS WEEK'S THREADS, TIED TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE IN-BETWEEN PERSON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one pull in you that hasn't gone away, a temper, a craving, a habit of the mind, and just see it, without scolding it or pretending it isn't there. Then remember the times you didn't follow it, even once: the pull is real, and you are still the one choosing. If you pray, you can hold the verse: the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart.
Tanya. Rabbi Shneur Zalman's book, named for its first word, on the in-between person who still feels the pull and does not obey it. Today's word.
Your line: the in-between person. The pull can stay, and still not be obeyed. See you soon.
